source: Goodwin and Wright (2001) Enhancing strategy evaluation in scenario planning: a role for decision analysis
finding: Abstract read via Crossref. Evaluating strategies across scenarios is the underdeveloped step of scenario planning. Informal evaluation can pick inferior strategies. They propose decision analysis to structure it.
numbers: No sample or effect size; conceptual paper. 176 citations in Crossref.
quote: if this is carried out informally then inferior strategies may be selected
limits: Abstract only; full text not opened. A proposal, not a test.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 7: add an explicit action-by-scenario robustness table instead of a narrative pick. No LLM test of it was reachable.

source: Wack (1985) Scenarios: Uncharted Waters Ahead (HBR landing page)
finding: Only the paywall intro was readable. It says forecasting worked reasonably in the stable 1950s-60s and that errors became frequent and sometimes dramatic after the early 1970s. Wack developed the Shell system with Edward Newland and taught scenario planning at Harvard Business School in 1983-84.
numbers: Dates only: early 1970s, Sept 1985 issue, HBS post 1983 and 1984. No steps, no counts.
limits: Full text paywalled. Gap 6 (what Shell did in 1972-73, which steps are original) NOT answered from the primary text.
agent_relevance: Confirms the framing 'forecasts fail, so reframe', which fits operator O1 (reframe the goal). Does not confirm the six-step recipe as Wack's.

source: Wack (1985) Scenarios: Shooting the Rapids (HBR landing page)
finding: Only the intro was readable. It repeats Wack's roles (head of Shell business environment division; developed the system with Newland). The visible text gives no method steps.
numbers: None beyond the roles and the 1983-84 HBS post.
limits: Paywalled. Nothing visible about 7-9 mini-scenarios or a cut to 2-3.
agent_relevance: The 'seven to nine, cut to two or three' step stays unverified as original Wack. Treat as later practitioner tidy-up until a primary text says otherwise.

source: Wilkinson and Kupers (2013) Living in the Futures (HBR landing page)
finding: Intro says Shell introduced the Unified Planning Machinery (UPM) in 1965, a computer-driven cash-flow planner. Executives found commitments ran past UPM's six-year horizon and UPM often erred even inside it. Shell shut UPM in the early 1970s. Wilkinson spent nearly a decade on Shell's scenario team.
limits: Intro only. The body on 1972-73 was not readable.
agent_relevance: Backstory: scenarios replaced a point-forecast machine. Supports a rule 'do not trust one projection when the horizon exceeds what the model can see'.

finding: Says Wack was first to use scenario planning in the private sector, at Shell London in the 1970s, and that Shell anticipated two Arab-induced oil shocks that decade. Cites his two 1985 HBR pieces and Chermack (2017). No method detail.
limits: Tertiary source. 'Anticipated the shocks' is not tested here; hindsight risk.
agent_relevance: No new support for the recipe. Points to Chermack 2017 for gap 6.

source: Chermack (2017) Foundations of Scenario Planning: The Story of Pierre Wack (Routledge)

limits: Not opened. Candidate source for gap 6.
agent_relevance: Next step: obtain the book chapters.

finding: Phelps, Chapman and Hidson 2001 did not surface in Crossref. The nearest hit was an Emerald executive briefing saying leaders gain from formal and informal scenario approaches to identify a range of possible futures. It states a benefit with no data, and may be a different document.
limits: Identity of the briefing unverified, so it is not cited as Phelps 2001. Treat as weak.
agent_relevance: Shows the pattern in this literature: benefits asserted, not measured.

finding: arXiv API returned HTTP 429, Semantic Scholar 429, OpenAlex 'insufficient budget', arxiv.org/search 429, and the WebSearch budget was used up. No new LLM paper could be found or opened for these gaps.

source: Design note, gap 2 (cut rule 7-9 to 2-3), from evidence already read
finding: No head-to-head found. Three candidate rules: Wack's two driver axes (importance x uncertainty), maximum-distance selection (Polyscene diversity planning), and self-ranking by the model. Infinity-Chat shows same-prompt similarity above 0.8, so self-ranking may keep near-duplicates.
agent_relevance: Test a maximum-distance embedding cut first; it is cheap and checkable.

source: Design note, gap 7 (robustness table), from Goodwin and Wright 2001 and K12
finding: An action-by-scenario table forces per-cell scoring instead of narrative preference. Earlier evidence (K12) says LLM-written coherence ratings are weak (accuracy 0.52-0.77), so cell scores need a second sample or an external check.
limits: Inference; no LLM test of the table.
agent_relevance: Implement as a testable arm: table vs no table at equal tokens.

source: Design note, gaps 9 and 10 (optimism bias, contrasting step), from Girona and Elbaum findings
finding: Girona workshops: 80% of scenarios mention technology, 61% techno-optimistic. Elbaum: targeted contrast gave -57% escalation vs -28% for a generic prompt, on one 7B model. Neither was tested on Claude-class models or outside the original task.
limits: Single model, one task each; not re-measured here.
agent_relevance: A forced opposite-sign driver per scenario is a cheap guard; its effect is unmeasured.

source: Design note, gap 4 (calibration), from Schoemaker 1993 and Phadnis 2015
finding: The human conflict (lab: overconfidence reduced; field: no aggregate change) is unresolved and abstract-level. For an LLM the test is Brier before vs after writing 2-3 scenarios on resolved questions. No source reached this session measures it.
agent_relevance: Run as an agent test; do not assume a calibration gain.

source: Crossref citation counts for the scenario literature (popularity, not effect)
finding: Counts read 2026-11-03: Cordova-Pozo 2023 review 173; Goodwin and Wright 2001 176; Meissner and Wulf 2013 124; 'Decision making and planning under low levels of predictability' 2009 206; 'The scenario planning paradox' 2018 60. These show attention, not effect size.
agent_relevance: The effect literature is thin; weight it lightly.
